items.title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
items.summary: This paper investigates quantum error correction using rotated surface-code memory implemented on a cloud-accessible superconducting processor, aiming to demonstrate logical error suppression scaling with code distance. The researchers optimized syndrome extraction circuits by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout, then ran memory experiments across varying code distances and up to many rounds of error correction. The optimized circuit significantly reduced per-round logical error rates compared to standard readout, and increasing the protected code distance produced clear error suppression with factors exceeding unity under maximum-likelihood decoding. However, performance varied across processor placements due to qubit quality differences, and long-memory experiments revealed persistent correlations suggesting a residual error component that weakens the distance advantage over many rounds. The work highlights how careful circuit compilation and hardware-aware optimization directly influence surface-code performance and motivates co-design of quantum processors and error-correction circuits for fault-tolerant computing on current cloud hardware.
items.citation: Shuwen Kan, Aaron Hoyt, Sean Garner et al.. Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
items.summary: This paper explores how AI agents can be used to find more efficient compilations of quantum circuits by exploiting classically verifiable structure in critical subroutines. When key circuit components are built from reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement-based uncomputation, their behavior on classical inputs can be efficiently simulated and verified through a fuzz-testing approach, enabling reliable certification of approximate circuit synthesis. The authors apply this paradigm to three practically important bottleneck subroutines: computing the inverse square root function relevant to Coulomb operator simulations for modeling inertial confinement fusion, decoding Reed-Solomon codes for a quantum interferometry algorithm, and implementing quantum look-up tables and Givens rotations for second-quantized quantum chemistry simulation. The paper presents reference implementations of these algorithms with explicit constraints designed to facilitate AI-driven optimization. These are offered as the basis for a competitive research challenge intended to accelerate community progress in AI-assisted quantum circuit compilation.

items.title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of computing the Bayesian evidence, the marginal likelihood of data under a model, which is critical for model comparison, goodness-of-fit testing, and detecting model misspecification in simulation-based inference settings. The authors propose ENFR (Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References), a method that learns Bayes factors relative to a flow-matched reference distribution and then recovers absolute evidence estimates in an amortized fashion, building on an existing Evidence Network framework. A key theoretical contribution is a novel neural network architecture, proven to jointly learn the individual evidences of multiple competing models simultaneously. Across a range of scientific benchmark applications, ENFR outperforms flow-based baselines and other density estimation approaches in accurately estimating the absolute evidence. The work also establishes that using the evidence as a test statistic yields a minimum-volume level-alpha test, making it a principled tool for assessing model fidelity prior to trusting parameter inference results.

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit for detecting respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus in children presenting to a pediatric emergency department with acute respiratory symptoms, using multiplex real-time PCR as the reference standard. In a prospective study of children aged eighteen years and younger, paired nasopharyngeal swabs were collected for simultaneous point-of-care rapid antigen testing and PCR analysis, with diagnostic performance assessed across age groups and clinical predictors of positivity identified through multivariable logistic regression. The rapid test demonstrated very high sensitivity and specificity for both pathogens, with excellent agreement with PCR results for adenovirus and RSV alike. RSV positivity was most common in infants under one year, while adenovirus peaked in school-aged children; conjunctival injection and fever independently predicted adenovirus positivity, whereas cough and age under one year predicted RSV positivity. The authors conclude that this dual-pathogen rapid test kit offers diagnostic accuracy comparable to PCR and may support timely clinical decision-making in pediatric emergency settings.
items.citation: Ates B, Kacar A, Kok S et al.. Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples. 2026

items.title: Point prevalence assessments of five respiratory viruses in adults ≥ 50 years of age in Germany by multi-pathogen rapid antigen testing on June 1, 2024, and December 15, 2024.
items.summary: This study investigated the prevalence and clinical impact of five respiratory viruses among community-dwelling adults aged fifty and older in Germany using two point-prevalence assessments conducted in summer and winter of 2024. Participants performed multi-pathogen rapid antigen self-tests capable of detecting adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus, and reported symptoms, healthcare use, and work absenteeism alongside the test results. The overall pathogen detection rate was low, with the majority of tests returning negative, but adenovirus was the most frequently detected pathogen at both time points, a finding that contrasts with its underrepresentation in routine surveillance systems. SARS-CoV-2 was associated with the greatest clinical burden, driving the highest rates of healthcare consultations and work absenteeism among those testing positive. The authors conclude that community-based self-testing can uncover asymptomatic reservoirs and underreported viral circulation, and that adenovirus may play a more prominent role as a co-infecting respiratory pathogen than currently recognized.

items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate article addresses a central controversy in exercise immunology: whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection, independent of confounding factors. The paper contrasts the broadly accepted view that moderate, short-duration exercise benefits immune defense with the contested claim that arduous exercise practiced by high-performance athletes and military personnel impairs immunity and elevates infection risk. Opposing groups debated whether athletes are genuinely more susceptible to infection than the general population, whether exercise alone can alter immunity independently of co-occurring stressors such as sleep disruption, anxiety, nutritional deficits, and environmental extremes, and whether the biomarkers and study designs used to support such claims are methodologically sound. Both sides agreed that infection susceptibility is multifactorial in origin, but disagreed on whether exercise per se constitutes an independent causative factor. The article concludes that this question remains unresolved and calls for more rigorous empirical research to disentangle the specific immunological effects of arduous exercise from the many other variables inherent to elite athletic and military populations.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process
items.summary: This paper describes the development and scope of the Rome V criteria for disorders of gut–brain interaction, which are gastrointestinal conditions arising from combinations of motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, altered gut microbiota, and changes in central nervous system processing. The Rome V process represented a comprehensive update to the prior Rome IV framework, synthesizing a decade of accumulated basic and clinical research into evidence-based revisions. Key advances include refined disorder definitions, expanded coverage of dietary, microenvironmental, pharmacogenomic, biopsychosocial, and sociocultural factors, as well as attention to gender and cross-cultural influences. The update also aimed to reduce stigmatizing terminology, improve diagnostic algorithms, better incorporate the patient illness experience, and revise therapeutic recommendations.
items.citation: Douglas A. Drossman, Lin Chang, Jan F. Tack. Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process. Gastroenterology. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search to gather existing evidence on exercise immunology across patient, recreationally active, and athlete populations with spinal cord injury. A central theme is that autonomic dysfunction following injury alters resting and post-exercise catecholamine concentrations, which may directly suppress immunity given that most lymphoid cells express adrenergic receptors, with this effect being especially pronounced in individuals with tetraplegia. However, the review also highlights that some immune responses, such as increases in natural killer cell cytotoxicity and mucosal immunity following exercise, appear partially independent of catecholamine changes and may resemble responses seen in able-bodied individuals, suggesting that compensatory mechanisms such as sympathetic reflex activity, receptor hypersensitivity, or neuroendocrine adjustments may offset injury-related immune deficits. The authors conclude that exercise and rehabilitation can improve certain measures of immunity and autonomic function after spinal cord injury, and call for further research to clarify the underlying mechanisms and implications for infection susceptibility.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria Louise Goosey-Tolfrey, NICOLETTE CLAIRE BISHOP. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper reviewed graft-versus-host disease, a potentially multi-systemic complication arising when donor lymphocytes attack host tissues following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with particular focus on its chronic form and associated physical impairments. The authors examined the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease alongside existing evidence from both animal and human studies on the effects of exercise in affected patients. Their review found that exercise training as an adjunct therapy shows promise for improving physical fitness and potentially immune function while reducing fatigue in transplant recipients. However, the authors conclude that the evidence base remains insufficient and that more randomized controlled trials specifically targeting patients with graft-versus-host disease are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: EHA Guidelines on management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Richter transformation
items.summary: This paper presents updated European clinical practice guidelines for the management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Richter transformation, developed under the European Hematology Association for the first time. The guidelines were produced through expert consensus across multiple European countries and, notably, incorporated patient advocacy representatives in their development. They adopt a holistic approach to disease management, spanning initial diagnosis and active surveillance through to treatment decisions informed by both disease- and patient-specific factors, and now explicitly address Richter transformation. Updated treatment recommendations include a recently approved time-limited combination therapy for first-line use and a continuous therapy option for patients who have been previously exposed to covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitors in the relapsed or refractory setting. The guidelines are intended to be updated annually to reflect the rapidly evolving landscape of CLL research and clinical practice.
items.citation: Barbara F. Eichhorst, Paolo Ghia, Francesc Bosch et al.. EHA Guidelines on management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Richter transformation. HemaSphere. 2026

items.title: Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae
items.summary: This paper investigated early-time photometric and spectroscopic properties of type II supernovae to determine whether photometric observations alone can identify those undergoing interaction with dense circumstellar material. The researchers assembled a large sample of type II supernovae, combining newly published events with literature objects, and classified them based on the presence or absence of transient narrow emission lines from highly ionised elements — known as "flash features" — detected in spectra taken within days of explosion. Through detailed analysis of light curves with near-daily cadence, the team found that supernovae exhibiting flash features are on average more luminous at peak, show longer rise times in the blue band, and are systematically bluer than their non-flash counterparts, with these colour differences likely reflecting intrinsic physical differences rather than dust extinction. A particularly diagnostic result was that colour-curve breaks occurring within the first month after explosion cleanly separate flash from non-flash supernovae, and when combined with peak absolute magnitude, provide a robust photometric indicator of circumstellar interaction. The study thus demonstrates that photometric data alone may suffice to identify supernovae interacting with dense circumstellar material, even without early spectroscopic observations.
items.citation: A. Mendez-Llorca, G. Folatelli, C. P. Gutierrez et al.. Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Entering the Era of Circumplanetary Ring Detection with Direct Imaging
items.summary: This paper investigated how circumplanetary ring systems would affect the detectability and photometric interpretation of exoplanets observed through direct imaging. The authors developed a hybrid forward model that combines a ray-casting approach for computing planet-ring mutual shadowing with empirical reflectance spectra derived from Cassini observations of Saturn's rings, applied to Jupiter-like planets hosting rings of varying size, inclination, and obliquity. Their simulations demonstrate that rings can substantially enhance planet-to-star flux ratios at favorable geometries, with Saturn-equivalent rings boosting peak flux significantly and more extended rings producing even greater contrast enhancements, while certain geometries can actually suppress total system brightness below that of a ringless planet. The team also identified multi-band photometry as a useful diagnostic tool for identifying exorings and applied their model to a specific directly imaged planet candidate to assess detectability prospects with an upcoming coronagraph instrument. They conclude that unaccounted-for ring systems could bias inferred planetary properties from direct imaging data, making it essential to incorporate ring effects into observation planning and interpretation as new direct imaging facilities come online.
items.citation: Samantha N. Hasler, Alexandra Z. Greenbaum, Geoffrey Bryden et al.. Entering the Era of Circumplanetary Ring Detection with Direct Imaging. arXiv. 2026

items.title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
items.summary: This paper investigates whether large language model agents can automate the assessment of reproducibility and analytical robustness in scientific research, using cancer registry studies as a test domain. The authors constructed a benchmark of published studies based on a major U.S. cancer registry database, pairing each paper with the data and resources needed to reproduce its findings. They developed an AI agent that successfully reproduced a substantial majority of atomic claims extracted from these papers, and built a second agentic pipeline that identifies underlying analytical choices, proposes defensible alternatives, and reruns analyses to test whether those choices alter conclusions. The robustness pipeline flagged a meaningful fraction of fully reproduced findings as potentially sensitive to analytical decisions, directing these cases toward expert review. The work demonstrates that LLM agents can meaningfully support scientific peer review by automating reproduction efforts and systematically probing the fragility of published conclusions.
items.citation: Shicheng Liu, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Andrew Drozdov et al.. AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
items.summary: This paper investigates quantum error correction using rotated surface-code memory implemented on a cloud-accessible superconducting processor. The researchers optimized syndrome extraction circuits by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout, then evaluated performance across multiple placements on the processor and over many error-correction rounds. The optimized circuit substantially reduced per-round logical error rates compared to standard readout approaches, with improvement factors differing between the X and Z bases, reflecting noise asymmetry in the hardware. Increasing the code distance while holding the other dimension fixed yielded clear logical error suppression, with error-suppression factors exceeding unity under maximum-likelihood decoding, demonstrating that logical errors can be suppressed beyond what a single code block achieves. However, performance degraded over longer experiments due to long-lived error correlations, pointing to persistent noise components that limit the benefit of increasing code distance and motivating closer co-design of quantum processors and error-correction circuits.
items.citation: Shuwen Kan, Aaron Hoyt, Sean Garner et al.. Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
items.summary: This paper explores a framework for using AI agents to discover more efficient compilations of quantum circuits by focusing on subroutines that possess classically verifiable structure. The key insight is that when critical circuit components are built from reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement-based uncomputation, their correctness can be efficiently checked by simulating execution on classical inputs, enabling a form of fuzz testing for approximate circuit synthesis. This verification capability allows AI agents to propose and certify circuit optimizations without requiring full quantum simulation. The approach is demonstrated across three application domains: computing an inverse square root function relevant to modeling inertial confinement fusion, decoding Reed-Solomon codes for a quantum interferometry algorithm, and implementing quantum look-up tables and Givens rotations for quantum chemistry simulations. The authors present reference implementations for these algorithms and frame the optimization challenge as a competition designed to accelerate AI-driven research into quantum circuit compilation.
items.citation: Tanuj Khattar, Nicholas C. Rubin, Craig Gidney et al.. Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI. arXiv. 2026

items.title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of computing the Bayesian evidence, the marginal likelihood of data under a model, which is essential for model comparison, goodness-of-fit testing, and detecting model misspecification in simulation-based inference settings. The authors develop ENFR (Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References), a method that learns Bayes factors relative to a flow-matched reference distribution and then recovers absolute evidence values in an amortized fashion, building on an existing Evidence Network framework. A key theoretical contribution is a proven neural network architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of multiple competing models simultaneously. The method is shown to outperform flow-based baselines and other density estimation approaches across a range of scientific benchmark applications, while also scaling favorably. By providing fast, accurate, amortized estimates of absolute evidence rather than mere evidence ratios, ENFR enables minimum-volume goodness-of-fit tests that are critical for validating the simulator models underlying simulation-based parameter inference.

items.title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis Detection with MiniDock MTB Using Swab Samples
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of MiniDock MTB, a novel test designed for detecting pulmonary tuberculosis in peripheral health settings where improved tools are urgently needed. Researchers conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study across seven countries, enrolling patients with presumptive pulmonary tuberculosis and testing them using both sputum swabs and tongue swabs, with culture-confirmed results serving as the reference standard and comparisons made against sputum-smear microscopy and the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay. MiniDock MTB achieved sensitivity above eighty-five percent with sputum swabs and nearly eighty percent with tongue swabs, with specificity exceeding ninety-seven percent for both sample types, closely matching the performance of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra while substantially outperforming smear microscopy. The test met World Health Organization accuracy targets for near-point-of-care tuberculosis diagnostics for both sputum and non-sputum samples, and usability assessments indicated the test was perceived as having good usability with no related adverse events reported. These findings suggest MiniDock MTB is a promising diagnostic tool suitable for diverse clinical settings, including those with limited resources.
items.citation: Seda Yerlikaya, Masuzyo Chirwa, Bukola Ajide et al.. Pulmonary Tuberculosis Detection with MiniDock MTB Using Swab Samples. New England Journal of Medicine. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviewed advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over a five-year period, synthesizing scientific evidence to inform updated WHO policy guidance that consolidates recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Key developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a frontline screening tool, the diversification of decentralised molecular diagnostics through multiple rapid nucleic acid amplification test platforms, and novel specimen types such as tongue swabs and stool samples that improve bacteriological confirmation in children and other populations unable to produce sputum. Drug-resistance testing has advanced through new molecular assays and targeted next-generation sequencing, now endorsed at reference laboratory level, while urine lipoarabinomannan assays offer diagnostic benefit primarily in people living with HIV who have advanced disease. Host blood transcriptomic and other biomarker signatures show promise for prognosis and triage, but no biomarker has yet met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from active disease, including subclinical tuberculosis. The authors conclude that significant performance, implementation, and equity gaps remain, identifying these as developmental priorities for the field.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives.
items.summary: This review examines the technological evolution and clinical deployment of molecular point-of-care testing platforms as diagnostics shift away from centralized laboratory settings. The authors systematically survey how modern platforms integrate isothermal nucleic acid amplification techniques, CRISPR-based detection systems, microfluidic chips, and smartphone-enabled digital interfaces to achieve automated, sample-to-answer diagnostics. These technologies have demonstrated broad clinical utility spanning infectious disease management, early cancer screening, cardiovascular triage, and metabolic disease monitoring. Despite substantial progress, the review identifies persistent barriers to widespread clinical adoption, including signal interference in multiplexed assays, enzyme instability without cold-chain infrastructure, high component costs, and insufficient regulatory frameworks. The authors argue that advances in synthetic biology, system integration, and artificial intelligence will be essential to realizing accessible and precise molecular diagnostics in resource-limited environments.
items.citation: Zhang D, Cui X, Zhang R et al.. Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives.. Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Smart electroactive molecularly imprinted polymers (e-MIPs) for precision diagnostics and point-of-care technologies: Design, mechanisms, and clinical translation.
items.summary: This review examines smart electroactive molecularly imprinted polymers, synthetic materials that combine selective molecular recognition with electrochemical signal transduction as alternatives to biological recognition elements like antibodies and enzymes. The authors critically evaluate recent progress in the design, synthesis, and operating principles of these materials, covering functional monomer selection, imprinting strategies, electropolymerization, and the incorporation of nanostructured and conductive nanomaterials to enhance analytical performance. Particular attention is given to how these materials are integrated into sensing platforms for infectious disease diagnostics, biomarker detection, wearable devices, and point-of-care technologies, with case studies demonstrating their capacity for rapid, label-free, and cost-effective analysis of real biological samples. The review also addresses persistent technical challenges, including binding-site heterogeneity, nonspecific adsorption, reproducibility, and scalability, alongside the hurdles remaining for clinical validation and translation.
items.venue: Advances in colloid and interface science

items.title: Predicted Preferences for Tuberculosis Point-of-Care Tests Among Tuberculosis-Affected Individuals in 5 High Burden Countries.
items.summary: This study investigated how individuals affected by tuberculosis value point-of-care diagnostic tests compared to standard facility-based testing across five high-burden countries. Using a discrete choice experiment methodology, researchers collected preference data from a large sample of tuberculosis-affected participants and applied simulations to model test preferences. The findings revealed that point-of-care tuberculosis tests were strongly preferred by affected individuals, even when those tests offered somewhat lower diagnostic accuracy than conventional facility-based alternatives. These results suggest that the convenience and accessibility of point-of-care testing may outweigh concerns about modest reductions in accuracy from the patient perspective, which has important implications for tuberculosis diagnostic policy and test development priorities.

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical translation. The authors synthesize multiomics approaches — including genome-wide association studies, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics — alongside advanced AI methods such as deep learning to analyze complex biological datasets underlying disease. The review covers applications spanning target identification and deconvolution, drug repositioning, de novo compound discovery, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Case studies in oncology, neurodegenerative diseases, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate how this convergence accelerates the drug development pipeline and enables more precise therapeutic interventions. The authors also acknowledge persistent challenges, including harmonization of heterogeneous omics data, reproducibility, and mitigation of algorithmic biases, while arguing that the fusion of these technologies marks a new era in bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: A framework for developing university policies on generative AI governance: a cross-national comparative study
items.summary: This study examined how universities across different national contexts are developing policies to govern generative AI in higher education, focusing on institutions in the United States, Japan, and China. The researchers conducted a cross-national comparative analysis of generative AI guidelines from leading universities in these three countries, applying an extended Technology Acceptance Model as an analytical lens across five domains and deriving twenty key themes through thematic coding. The analysis revealed distinct national policy orientations, with American universities emphasizing faculty autonomy and adaptability, Japanese universities prioritizing ethics and risk management in alignment with government guidance, and Chinese universities reflecting a centralized model focused on technology application and integration. Based on these comparative findings, the researchers proposed the University Policy Development Framework for Generative AI, which integrates technological, organizational, and social dimensions to help institutions balance innovation against risk. The framework is intended to support universities in assessing policy priorities and building institutional capacity for sustainable generative AI governance.
items.citation: Ming Li, Qin Xie, Ariunaa Enkhtur et al.. A framework for developing university policies on generative AI governance: a cross-national comparative study. Studies in Higher Education. 2026

items.title: Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective
items.summary: This paper examines the regulatory landscape surrounding cell-derived extracellular vesicles as therapeutic and diagnostic agents, focusing on how their acellular nature creates classification difficulties across existing pharmaceutical frameworks. The authors analyzed how major regulatory jurisdictions, including the European Union, United States, and Japan, currently approach these products, noting that a recent European guidance document has explicitly placed minimally modified extracellular vesicles outside the advanced therapy medicinal products category while the United States treats them as drugs and biological products. The review identifies consequent challenges in regulatory positioning, quality assessment, comparability, and cross-regional clinical development arising from this jurisdictional heterogeneity. The authors argue that extracellular vesicle products can and should be developed within existing medicinal product frameworks such as biologics, provided that regulatory tools are applied consistently and ambiguous areas such as classification criteria, critical quality attributes, potency strategies, and comparability approaches are resolved through clarification rather than new normative frameworks. The work is positioned as a synthesis intended to support regulatory dialogue among international agencies and scientific societies to advance these therapies toward safe, reproducible, and internationally credible clinical application.
items.citation: Tania Limongi, Paola Milla, Barbara Stella et al.. Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective. Journal of Extracellular Vesicles. 2026

items.title: Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae
items.summary: This study examined early-time photometric and spectroscopic properties of Type II supernovae to investigate signatures of interaction with dense circumstellar material. The researchers combined newly observed supernovae from the Precision Observations of Infant Supernova Explosions collaboration with a literature sample, assembling a large dataset with high-cadence, high-precision multi-band photometry and spectra taken within four days of estimated explosion. Supernovae were classified based on whether they displayed transient narrow emission lines from highly ionised elements, known as flash features, which indicate early-phase interaction with circumstellar material. Flash supernovae were found to be more luminous at peak, tend toward longer rise times in the blue band, and are systematically bluer than non-flash events, with these colour differences at around twenty days post-explosion reflecting intrinsic physical differences rather than dust extinction. Crucially, the study demonstrates that colour-curve breaks occurring within thirty days of explosion, combined with peak absolute magnitude, provide a robust photometric diagnostic capable of identifying circumstellar interaction even when early spectroscopic observations are unavailable.
items.citation: A. Mendez-Llorca, G. Folatelli, C. P. Gutierrez et al.. Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification
items.summary: This paper investigated multi-label classification of retinal fundus diseases, where images often exhibit multiple simultaneous conditions and available datasets are heterogeneous with severe class imbalance. The researchers constructed a unified label space spanning nearly forty disease targets by combining three public fundus datasets, then compared three architectural approaches sharing a common backbone: a three-stage gated cascade mimicking clinical triage, a flat multi-label classifier, and a label-correlation model using a transformer decoder with learned label queries. Error tracing revealed that the coarse screening and routing stages in the cascade discarded a substantial proportion of true disease instances, causing the staged pipeline to underperform relative to its complexity. Label-correlation modeling provided the largest single architectural gain, and blending the flat and label-correlation models with test-time augmentation achieved the best overall performance across the majority of evaluated metrics, particularly for low-prevalence pathologies. The study also identified that ensembling cascaded models with continuous-output models is detrimental, and that per-source negative sampling is necessary to eliminate a dataset-specific shortcut that otherwise produces artificially perfect discrimination.
items.citation: Md Asif Uddin, Jannatul Ferdous, Asif Islam et al.. Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification. arXiv. 2026

items.title: LagNet: Lag-Structured Operators for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: The paper investigates long-term time series forecasting by examining the structural form of the history-to-future mapping operator rather than focusing solely on input representations or model architectures. The authors observe that sensitivity matrices across diverse model families consistently display diagonal patterns corresponding to relative temporal lags, motivating a lag-structured approach to forecasting. They introduce LagLayer, a building block that constructs a Toeplitz matrix by tying history-to-future connections sharing the same relative lag while incorporating scaling coefficients to allow flexibility, enabling it to replace standard temporal linear layers in existing models. Stacking multiple LagLayer modules with nonlinear activations and feature maps produces LagNet. Experiments on standard benchmarks show the approach is competitive with strong baselines, and additional diagnostics and limited-data experiments demonstrate that the lag-structured design is both effective and sample-efficient compared to unconstrained linear layers.
items.citation: Zhenan Yu, Guangxin Jiang, Jiuyun Jiang et al.. LagNet: Lag-Structured Operators for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Synthetic Image Oversampling for Rare-Class Representation Learning in Deep Facial Phenotyping
items.summary: This paper investigated whether synthetic facial images can improve deep learning models for recognizing rare genetic syndromes, where patient data are scarce and imbalanced across disorders. The researchers used disease-specific synthetic oversampling by augmenting a genomic facial image database with synthetically generated images, then evaluated the effect at increasing augmentation levels on two models — an image-based and a multimodal approach — using fixed real-data training and evaluation partitions. They assessed both overall recognition accuracy and disorder-specific performance, complemented by an analysis of how class structure in the embedding space changed with augmentation. Synthetic oversampling improved mean recognition accuracy in both models, though gains were modest for the image-based model and more sustained for the multimodal one, and were accompanied by uneven responses across individual disorders, including accuracy reductions for some conditions. The authors conclude that synthetic augmentation can benefit rare-class facial phenotyping but that the appropriate amount and which disorders actually gain must be evaluated on a per-disorder basis within each specific training setup.
items.citation: Miles Liao, Zhanliang Wang, Hongzhuo Chen et al.. Synthetic Image Oversampling for Rare-Class Representation Learning in Deep Facial Phenotyping. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Escaping Parameter Space: Tight Generalization Bounds via Representation Quality
items.summary: This paper develops a generalization bound for deterministic neural networks that operates in representation space rather than parameter space, using the quality of last hidden layer representations as measured by a parameter-free nearest-neighbor classifier. The bound avoids traditional complexity measures such as weight norms, KL divergences, or compression schemes, and instead decomposes additively into three independently measurable empirical quantities: local class geometry, decoder-network agreement, and training stability. Applied to standard benchmarks, the bound achieves notably tight certificates, including the first non-vacuous guarantees on a large-scale hundred-class dataset when trained from scratch, and very small gaps when using pretrained frozen representations on datasets up to a thousand classes. Using the bound as a diagnostic tool, the authors demonstrate that deliberately degrading local class geometry in representations eliminates generalization while preserving dataset memorization, establishing class geometry as a causally relevant mechanism for generalization rather than merely a correlate. The work also offers an explanation for why parameter-space certificates tend to be loose, showing that learned representations are substantially more robust to weight perturbations than linear readout layers.
items.citation: Niclas Göring, Shuofeng Zhang, Branton DeMoss et al.. Escaping Parameter Space: Tight Generalization Bounds via Representation Quality. arXiv. 2026

items.title: A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster
items.summary: This study presents a large-scale spectroscopic survey of the Orion Nebula Cluster aimed at identifying and characterizing its pre-main-sequence stellar population. Using low-resolution optical spectroscopy from MMT/Hectospec, the researchers derived spectral types, youth indicators, and accretion diagnostics for over a thousand stars in the cluster region, then combined these data with kinematic membership analysis from Gaia astrometry to confirm cluster membership. Infrared photometry from the Spitzer Space Telescope was used to build a census of protoplanetary disks, while stellar masses, ages, and extinctions were estimated using a dedicated code that incorporates photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models and Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation. The outcome is a homogeneous catalog of confirmed T Tauri stars with comprehensive spectroscopic, kinematic, disk, and physical parameter characterizations. This catalog is presented as a robust foundation for future investigations into the cluster's kinematic structure, age distribution, and protoplanetary disk population.
items.citation: Jesús Hernández, Ezequiel Manzo-Martínez, Lucía Adame et al.. A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Observation of relativistic bond weakening in seaborgium hexacarbonyl
items.summary: This paper investigated the chemical bonding properties of seaborgium hexacarbonyl, a complex formed by the superheavy element seaborgium, to probe how relativistic quantum effects influence metal-ligand stability at the heaviest elements. Using gas chromatography experiments, researchers measured the formation yields of seaborgium and tungsten hexacarbonyl complexes to determine the first bond dissociation energy of seaborgium hexacarbonyl. The study found that the first bond dissociation energy of seaborgium hexacarbonyl is lower than that of tungsten hexacarbonyl, reversing the otherwise increasing trend in bond dissociation energies seen across the lighter group 6 hexacarbonyls. This weakening of the metal-carbonyl bond is attributed to relativistic destabilization of the 6d atomic orbitals in seaborgium, and the experimental result agrees with state-of-the-art theoretical predictions. The work provides direct experimental evidence that relativistic effects can measurably weaken chemical bonding in superheavy element compounds.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it provides direct experimental evidence that relativistic effects measurably weaken chemical bonds in a superheavy element compound, demonstrating that seaborgium hexacarbonyl has a lower bond dissociation energy than its lighter homologue — a striking deviation from expected periodic trends.
items.citation: Alexander Yakushev, Jadambaa Khuyagbaatar, Christoph E. Düllmann et al.. Observation of relativistic bond weakening in seaborgium hexacarbonyl. Nature. 2026

items.title: RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles
items.summary: This paper investigated how RNA achieves catalytic activity through dynamic structural changes, focusing on the interplay between RNA conformation and magnesium ion binding, which had not previously been characterized at near-atomic resolution. Using a heterogeneity-focused cryo-electron microscopy data analysis protocol designed for conformationally flexible RNA particles, the researchers determined structural ensembles of RNase P RNA comprising dozens of coexisting active and inactive conformers that differ in a transient tertiary interaction essential for catalytic activity. They found that an accessory protein does not alter local RNA structure but instead induces thermodynamic allostery that enhances catalysis by modulating the dynamics of this tertiary interaction. Four distinct classes of magnesium ions were identified as playing critical roles in governing the structure, dynamics, and catalysis of these conformational ensembles. The findings challenge the conventional view of a single static catalytic structure, instead establishing a paradigm in which RNA catalysis is regulated through multimodal communications coupled to the dynamics of RNA–magnesium conformational ensembles.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals that RNA catalytic activity is not fixed but arises from shifting populations of active and inactive structural states, with magnesium ions and accessory proteins playing key roles in controlling which conformations dominate.
items.citation: Maximilia F. S. Degenhardt, Hermann F. Degenhardt, Bapurao A. Bhoge et al.. RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles. Nature. 2026

items.title: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
items.summary: This paper reports the realization of an optical nuclear clock based on the thorium-229 isotope, which possesses a uniquely low-energy nuclear transition accessible to lasers. The researchers stabilized a continuous-wave laser to the thorium-229 nuclear transition at approximately 148 nm using absorption spectroscopy with rapid feedback, with the nuclei embedded in a room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal, and compared a subharmonic of the clock laser to an established single-ion optical clock. The nuclear clock demonstrated shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability that approaches the level of state-of-the-art atomic clocks over a day of averaging, with projections for further improvements of several orders of magnitude in future devices. Beyond demonstrating the clock itself, the authors applied it to constrain models of ultralight dark matter by searching for periodic fluctuations and slow drifts in the nuclear transition energy, finding that the enhanced sensitivity of the thorium-229 transition yields competitive or superior constraints compared to the best atomic clocks for dark matter coupling to both photons and the strong force.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it demonstrates a functioning nuclear clock by directly locking a laser to a nuclear transition in thorium-229, representing a major step toward a new class of timekeeping device based on atomic nuclei rather than electron transitions. The use of a rapid feedback loop based on absorption spectroscopy makes the system practical and operational in a continuous-wave regime.
items.citation: L. Toscani De Col, T. Riebner, I. Morawetz et al.. A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop. Nature. 2026

items.title: A nuclear clock synchronized to 229Th
items.summary: This paper demonstrates the first operational nuclear clock based on the uniquely low-energy isomeric transition in thorium-229, a long-sought milestone in precision timekeeping. The researchers stabilized a continuous-wave vacuum-ultraviolet laser to a resolved nuclear transition in thorium-229 embedded in calcium fluoride crystals, using a vacuum-ultraviolet source generated by four-wave mixing in cadmium vapor and a frequency modulation absorption readout scheme to create a fast, high-signal-to-noise frequency discriminator. The resulting clock achieves a fractional frequency instability that improves with averaging time, and measurements performed on two independently fabricated crystals agree at a level consistent with earlier comb-based spectroscopy on similar crystals. These results establish that laser-addressed atomic nuclei can serve as genuine, reproducible clock references, opening a path toward compact solid-state nuclear clocks and sensitive probes of fundamental physics that go beyond what electronic-transition atomic clocks can offer.
items.why_notable: This work draws attention because it demonstrates that laser-addressed atomic nuclei can serve as functional timekeeping references, establishing a solid-state material as a viable platform for compact nuclear clocks and quantum sensors—a long-sought milestone in precision measurement.
items.citation: Beichen Huang, Gaowei Yan, Qi Xiao et al.. A nuclear clock synchronized to 229Th. Nature. 2026
